system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2122-03-23 04:28:00 to 2122-04-01 17:18:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of CAD, CABG, COPD, esophagitis, and alcohol abuse was admitted for chest pain that occurred while attempting to eat spinach, which he felt stuck in his throat, followed by vomiting and chest pressure. Initial evaluation ruled out acute cardiac ischemia with normal troponins and non-diagnostic EKG changes. A CT abdomen showed no acute surgical process but noted a stable moderate-to-severe SMA stenosis and a hiatal hernia. An EGD revealed severe esophageal ulceration and a 9 mm stricture at the gastroesophageal junction, which was dilated to 12 mm. His chest pain was attributed to esophageal pathology rather than cardiac causes. He was managed with acid suppression, including a switch from omeprazole to sublingual lansoprazole for better compliance, and a soft diet. He remained stable, with no arrhythmias or respiratory deterioration, and was discharged home with plans for outpatient EGD follow-up and continued medication management.
problems: Diaphragmatic hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
Family history of ischemic heart disease

# N/V/chest and abd pain: One week after esophageal stricture 
dilatation in patient with continued EtOH abuse and history of 
ulcerative esophagitis.  The exam was concerning for 
mediasteinitis with CT scan confirming esophagitis and 
mediasteinitis. This was supported by lactate, leukocytosis and 
low grade fever. There was concern for microperforation even

however there was still some worry that there could have been a 
microperforation that was not observed radiographically. An EGD 
was not done given the risk of perforation. Blood cultures were 
drawn, and he was started on ceftriaxone and flagyl to cover for 
translocation (10 day course). He was kept NPO, and was started 
on TPN for nutritional support. He has since been strictly NPO 
with TPN for a week to try and decrease the inflammation 
surrounding the esophagus. He was reimaged to reevaluate his 
esophagus, and CT ___ showed marked interval improvement in 
degree of esophageal wall thickening and periesophageal fat 
stranding, consistent with improving esophagitis. He was put on 
a sips trial which he successfully passed. He has done well so 
far and continues with sips of light clear fluids, but will 
remain on TPN until he is able to take in all of his nutritional 
support.  GI did NOT want any PO medications until he follows up 
in outpatient GI clinic, and all medications were given by IV 
form.

___ tear was also a possibility. He had guiac positive 
stools, which later resolved.

bleeding. He was followed on telemetry, his home diltiazem was 
held and was covered with IV metoprolol. He was taken off of 
metoprolol as HR was <100 without need for rate control.  He was 
discharged off all nodal agents.

further hypoxia. We continued O2 supplement, as well as his home 
tiotropium, fluticasone, and albuterol.

in outpatient GI clinic, and all medications were given by IV

# PAF: Reported self limited atrial flutter in the ED, resolved

INDICATION:  ___ male with history of cirrhosis, presents with fever
and vomiting as well as chest pain.

___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were acquired from the lung bases through the pubic
symphysis following administration of intravenous, without oral contrast due
to intolerance.  Multiplanar reformations were generated.

CT CHEST:  There is no evidence of pneumomediastinum.  Note is made of
circumferential mural thickening and mucosal hyperemia along the mid-to-lower
esophagus extending to the level fo the gastroesophageal junction, with mild
surrounding inflammation.  There is increase in mediastinal lymphadenopathy in
the paratracheal, pretracheal, precarinal, and subcarinal location up to 13
mm, likely reactive.  

There is no axillary adenopathy.  Although not tailored for evaluation of
pulmonary embolism, there are no large central filling defects to suggest
pulmonary embolism.  There is biapical pulmonary scarring.  Patchy right upper
lobe reticular opacity slight more prominent since ___, nonspecific. 
Predominantly right-sided paraseptal emphysematous changes are present.  There
are trace left greater than right effusions.  Bibasilar dependent atelectasis
is noted.  Central airways remain patent.

The heart is normal in size without pericardial effusion.  Multivessel
coronary arterial and aortic valve calcifications are noted.

CT ABDOMEN:  The liver appears mildly lobulated without definite focal lesion.
The gallbladder contains a stone without evidence of cholecystitis.  The
spleen and adrenal glands are unremarkable.  The pancreas appears diffusely
atrophic.  Bilateral kidneys enhance symmetrically without hydronephrosis or
hydroureter, containing multiple cysts, some of which are too small to fully
characterize, the largest cyst measuring 2.8 cm on the right.  There is a
small axial hiatal hernia.  Small and large bowel loops are normal in caliber.
There is no evidence of obstruction.  No free air or free fluid.  Scattered
diverticulosis of the colon is seen without diverticulitis.  No mesenteric
adenopathy.

Great vessels are patent although moderate atherosclerotic calcifications are
seen involving the descending aorta with extension into left greater than
right renal arteries and celiac trunk and SMA.

CT PELVIS:  The bladder is massively distended and decompression should be
considered.  The rectum and prostate appear within normal limits.  No pelvic
sidewall or inguinal adenopathy.  No free fluid in the pelvis.

BONE WINDOW:  No focal concerning lesion.  Moderate multilevel thoracolumbar
spondylosis, disc space narrowing, and endplate sclerosis is present.  The
patient is status post median sternotomy.  Minimal retrolisthesis is present
at L5-S1.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Circumferential esophageal wall thickening and hyperemia of mid-to-lower
esophagus extending to the GE junction with paraesophageal stranding,
consistent with esophagitis.   Increased mediastinal stranding and adenopathy
suggest mediastinitis.  No pneumomediastinum to indicate frank perforation,
though microperforation cannot be excluded.  History of recent endoscopy and
dilation was obtained later. 

2.  No bowel obstruction.

3.  Cholelithiasis.

4.  Trace left pleural effusion.  Right predominant emphysema.

5.  Renal cysts.

6.  Trace pleural effusions, new on the left since ___.

Findings reported to Dr. ___ via phone at 8:30 a.m. on ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ male with ulcerative esophagitis with nausea,
vomiting, and chest pain and esophageal inflammation on CT.  Evaluate for
perforation.

COMPARISON:  CT ___.  The report from endoscopies ___ and ___
were reviewed in the ___ medical record.  

SINGLE CONTRAST ESOPHAGRAM: Spot fluoroscopic images were obtained while
patient is ingesting Optiray.  Contrast passes freely through the esophagus
without evidence of hold up.  No leak is detected to suggest esophageal
perforation.  No large stricture is identified.  The stomach empties promptly

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of esophageal perforation.

HISTORY:  New right PICC line.

CHEST, SINGLE AP PORTABLE VIEW.

A right subclavian PICC line is present.  The tip overlies the right IJ vein
at the level of the mid cervical spine.  No pneumothorax is detected.  

This finding was discussed by radiology resident, M. ___, with ___

CHEST, SINGLE AP VIEW.

A right subclavian PICC line is present.  The tip extends cephalad and

Again seen is hyperinflation, sternotomy wires, prominence  of

PICC REPLACEMENT

INDICATION:  ___ man with severe esophagitis and mediastinitis who
requires TPN.  Need to advance the midline PICC line into the central
position.

OPERATORS:  ___, M.D.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  The procedure was explained to the patient.  The
patient was brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the
angiographic table.  The existing PICC line in the right arm was prepped and
draped in usual sterile fashion.  Initial scout fluoroscopic images
demonstrated the tip of the PICC line in the right axillary vein.  The
existing PICC line was cut and a nitinol wire was placed through and navigated
into the SVC.  The old PICC line was removed.  A peel-away sheath was placed
over the wire.  Through the peel-away sheath, a new double lumen Power PICC
line measuring 38.5 cm length was then placed.  The wire and the peel-away
sheath were removed.  The distal tip of the PICC line is in the distal SVC. 
Both lumens flushed easily.  Sterile dressings were applied.  The patient
tolerated the procedure well.  No immediate post-procedure complications were
noted.

IMPRESSION:  Successful replacement of the existing PICC line.  Currently, the
distal tip of the PICC line is in distal SVC.  The final length of the PICC
line is 38.5 cm.  The catheter is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You were brought in last night with nausea, vomiting, and chest and belly pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been feeling sick for a few days. I couldn’t keep anything down. And my chest hurts when I breathe. I did have a few beers that morning, but I’ve been drinking like that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The team noted you mentioned vomiting blood. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, once. I thought it might be from my stomach issues. I’ve had trouble with that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows esophagitis and a recent dilation. We did a CT scan last night, and it shows significant inflammation in your esophagus and the area around it in the chest — that’s called mediastinitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mediastinitis? That sounds serious. Is it from the dilation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. The inflammation could be from the procedure, especially since you’ve continued drinking. We’re worried there might have been a tiny tear — a microperforation — but the scan didn’t show a big hole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Could that make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a concern, yes. That’s why we’re not letting you eat or drink anything right now — we need to let your esophagus rest and heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nothing at all? Not even water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. You’ll get nutrition through an IV line — we call it TPN. It will keep you nourished while your esophagus heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I guess I don’t have a choice. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped your oral medications for now — things like Prevacid, sucralfate, and diltiazem — because we don’t want you swallowing pills. But we’re giving you IV versions of some, like levothyroxine and pantoprazole, to keep your conditions managed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I felt my pulse racing in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a brief episode of atrial flutter — a fast heart rhythm. It resolved on its own after fluids. We’re watching it on telemetry. We’ve paused your diltiazem and are using IV metoprolol only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Usually it settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep monitoring. Now, we also started antibiotics — ceftriaxone and metronidazole — to cover for infection, since mediastinitis can be dangerous if untreated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics? So it’s an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The inflammation could let bacteria spread. We’re treating it as if there might be infection until we’re sure it’s under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least a week, probably more. We’ll repeat the CT in a few days to see if the inflammation is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line in your arm so we can give you the antibiotics and TPN safely. The first one wasn’t in the right spot, so we fixed it this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why they were adjusting the line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Now it’s in the right place — in the big vein near your heart — and working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still no food, but the chest pain is better. I’m tired of being NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your labs are improving — your white count is coming down, and your lactate normalized. That’s a good sign the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any word on the heart rhythm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No further episodes. Your heart rate is stable, so we’ve stopped the IV metoprolol. You’re off all heart rate meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll repeat the CT scan in a couple of days to check your esophagus. Once we see improvement, we’ll try small sips of clear fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — the new CT shows marked improvement. The swelling in your esophagus has gone down a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips of water today. If you tolerate that, we’ll slowly advance to clear liquids. But you’ll still need TPN for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it. Anything to get off the IV nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the sips. No pain, no vomiting. We’ll keep you on clear liquids for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not quite yet. You’ll need to go to an extended care facility for a bit. You’ll continue IV antibiotics and TPN, and we’ll make sure you’re safe to swallow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was hoping to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know, but you still need IV meds and nutrition. The rehab team will help you transition safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed some bacteria, but it’s likely not a real infection. We don’t need to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need. Your other labs are stable. Hemoglobin is steady — no more bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my COPD? I’m on oxygen here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your oxygen and inhalers going. Your breathing is stable, no wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go to rehab tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue IV pantoprazole, antibiotics for two more days, and TPN. Oxygen and inhalers too. The heparin shots are for blood clot prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re stopped for now. You’ll restart them only after your GI follow-up in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. You’ve done well — pain gone, eating sips, inflammation down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Just want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You will. Keep with the rehab team, follow up with GI, and please — no alcohol. It’s making your condition worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll try. It’s hard, but I see what it’s doing to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. A social worker will connect you with support services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and good luck at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update — your discharge meds are set. The heparin will be stopped once you’re at rehab, as per our call with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So I won’t need those shots long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just until you’re moving well. The rest — antibiotics, pantoprazole, TPN — will continue as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve made great progress. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Any last questions before you go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Just want to rest and heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve earned it. We’ll be in touch with the rehab team. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Safe travels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — your transfer to rehab was smooth, and they’ve accepted your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they got me settled. They’re going over my meds now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember — no oral meds until GI says so, and keep with the TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart choice. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your blood cultures were negative, so no bloodstream infection. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All signs point to recovery. Keep following up, and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check-in. You’re officially discharged. We’ll send all records to rehab and your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll make sure to keep my follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe stay at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Goodbye for now.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of alcohol abuse, COPD, CAD s/p CABG, and esophageal stricture was admitted for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and hematemesis. He had recently undergone esophageal dilation and presented with signs of esophagitis and mediastinitis on CT imaging. Due to concern for microperforation, he was kept NPO and started on IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole) and TPN for nutritional support. An upper GI series ruled out frank perforation. His atrial flutter resolved with hydration, and he was managed without anticoagulation. Repeat CT showed marked improvement in esophageal inflammation, allowing a trial of sips, which he tolerated. He was discharged to extended care with plans to continue IV pantoprazole, antibiotics, and TPN, with follow-up in the GI clinic to reassess oral intake and medication restart.
